analysis.title: The Pulse of the Market: Close to a Crossroads
key_insights: RBC's tiers of fear, sentiment and valuation work suggest US stocks could stabilize soon, even if Thursday's close (11/5) is not the low. Indicators are not 'washed out', so fundamentals and earnings still matter into early 2027.

The S&P 500 closed 5.9% below its most recent all-time high on 11/5, a second tier 1 (5-10%) pullback this year after the 9.1% drawdown from the late-January peak to the late-March low. Tier 1 equivalent S&P levels are 7,037-7,428.

Base case: the pullback stays in tier 1 and the S&P 500 does not fall below 7,000. RBC is not calling for a tier 2 (14-20%, 6,255-6,724) but is watching AI regulation risk to earnings and the economy, which it expects to linger into early 2027.
The 'moment of truth' is expected in early 1Q27 reporting season, when companies issue year-ahead outlooks. Company commentary may stay subdued until mid-January.

AAII net bulls were -14.3% on the weekly reading (prior week -3.6%) and -7.43% on the four-week average (prior week -3.53%). The four-week average sits between the long-term average and -1 standard deviation, a zone followed on average by an 11% (11.1% in the sentiment model) 12-month forward S&P gain. Institutional client tone is 'stunned' rather than 'panicked'.

The US vs non-US developed market relative NTM P/E is back at post-COVID lows after US underperformance since early October. RBC says to be on guard for another bout of US and big-cap growth/AI leadership if a catalyst arrives.

Bottom-up forward P/Es for the S&P 500 and Nasdaq 100 are near or below post-2022 lows, including April 2025. Market-cap-weighted S&P 500 NTM P/E fell from 27.3 (1/28/26) to 20.6 (11/5/26), a 24.5% compression that exceeds the typical major-drawdown compression (median -20.5%).

Russell 2000 forward P/Es are at or slightly below early-2026 Iran war lows but well above April 2025 lows. The Russell 2000 market-cap-weighted FY2 P/E broke below 13x in April 2025, a reliable bottom signal, and RBC does not see that now. This tempers its enthusiasm.

Earnings sentiment needs to stabilize for P/Es to stop falling. Upward EPS revision rates correlate with forward P/Es, and revisions have decelerated in recent months, though the S&P 500 gauge has stopped trending lower in the latest update.

Clients flagged that Texas data center builds will be more expensive and slower but not stopped, and that AI capex/policy risk may hit 2028 EPS more than 2027. RBC agrees and says the AI policy risk to earnings is just starting as a conversation.

RBC continues to prefer Small Caps to Large Caps (outperforming since mid-October, briefly stumbled after midterms, rebounded after Friday's strong October NFP). The call depends on high yield spreads and VIX staying contained, and on economic optimism building. Small Caps may not lead in outright derisking.

Sector valuation model: most expensive are Industrials, Utilities and Consumer Discretionary. Consumer Staples, Comm Services and Energy look attractive, Tech is modestly attractive. RBC is overweight Financials (cyclicality) and Health Care (defense), underweight Utilities.

Semis FY2 P/E (R3000 Semis & Semi Equipment) broke below its five-year and long-term averages on a median basis (long-term average 18.7, post-2020 average 21.4). Trough levels remain elusive, and the drop in revisions reflects expected downward revisions that may prove wrong.

Midterm read-through: Tech, Comm Services and Utilities connect to AI views. Energy and Consumer Staples/Discretionary tie to the Iran war, tariffs and cost of living. Health Care and Industrials (tariffs) matter less. Consensus expects a divided government with a Democratic Congress to accomplish little because of Presidential veto.

Sector sensitivity work since COVID: Financials and Consumer Discretionary outperform when gas and diesel prices fall, Energy and Tech lag. Energy and Tech also lag when rates fall while most other sectors outperform. Consumer Discretionary, Staples, Financials, Health Care, Materials and Real Estate lead when consumer confidence rises.
Historically, when the S&P was not down in either 3Q or 4Q of a midterm year, the following year's return averaged 6.2% (median 3.5%) vs 16.9% average after all midterms. 3Q26 was +2.0%.
Past three midterm elections were associated with tier 1 or tier 2 drawdowns, so the 5.9% drop is in line with typical election volatility.

Bottom-up consensus S&P 500 EPS: trailing 4Q level $355 for 4Q26 (calendar 2026), up from $313 at the start of the year. Trailing EPS growth 28% for 4Q26 (13% in 2025) and 20% for 4Q27. Revenue growth 14%. 2027 EPS growth forecast ticked down while 2026 moved up.

Consensus net income growth: S&P 500 peaks in 2026 and decelerates in 2027-2028. AI basket 4Q26 growth 56%, Small Caps 50%, S&P 500 28%, ex-AI 21%. For 4Q27: AI basket 38%, Small Caps 37%, S&P 500 20%, ex-AI 11%. RBC sees deceleration of non-Mag 7 and non-AI cohorts in 2027-2028 as a knock against the broadening trade.

Upward EPS revisions: S&P 500 at 59.3% and Russell 2000 at 52.8%. Top-10 names ticked up to 59% from 54% (near past highs around 90% earlier) and ex-top-10 fell to 51% before returning to 59%, so the gap has closed.
Sector revision profiles: strongest EPS and sales revisions in Energy and Tech for both Large and Small Cap. Consumer Discretionary is the only Large Cap sector with negative EPS and sales revisions.

Performance since the early-October tech peak: Staples has outperformed most, Health Care second, Tech and Comm Services the only underperformers. Post-midterms Comm Services leads and Energy lags most, with Tech and Industrials also lagging.
VIX returned to 28 this week, just short of the Iran war high of about 30. High yield spreads have widened only very slightly.
Growth/value has tracked 10-year yields since late summer: Growth outperformed as yields rose, Value as yields fell, and this held post-midterms.

earnings_insights: Bottom-up consensus S&P 500 EPS (Bloomberg) is $355 trailing 4Q for 4Q26 (calendar 2026), up from $313 at the start of 2026, forecast not yet reported.
Consensus trailing 4Q EPS growth is 28% for 4Q26 vs 13% for 2025, slowing to 20% for 4Q27. Revenue growth is 14%. These are consensus estimates.
Consensus single-quarter EPS growth: 3Q26 about 33-34% and still rising, 4Q26 about 29-30% and flat. Consensus 3Q26 S&P 500 growth rate level 33.1, 2026 29.8, 2027 20.3.

S&P 500 net income is expected by consensus to peak in 2026 growth and decelerate in 2027 and 2028. The AI basket is now expected to peak in 2026 growth, a new development during 2Q26 reporting season.
Consensus 3Q26 EPS growth improved most for Energy since 10/2/26. Consumer Discretionary, Comm Services and Industrials improved modestly but remain below the market.
Upward EPS revisions rose slightly for the S&P 500 and Russell 2000 in the latest update. RBC flags the risk of downward revisions as year-ahead outlooks arrive in early 1Q27.
RBC warns that bottom-up 2027 EPS growth forecasts may be too high, noting 2019 and 2023 forecasts were cut after the 2018 tariffs and 2022 Russia-Ukraine war.

AAII net bulls -14.3% weekly and -7.43% four-week average, between the long-term average and -1 standard deviation. The weekly reading is near most post-2025 tariff lows but not the Iran war low.
Small Caps tend to underperform when volatility rises and when high yield spreads widen. Spreads have widened only very slightly.

geopolitical: The Iran war is lasting longer than companies anticipated and is a concern for Energy, consumer sectors, and the inflation outlook.
Midterm election outcome: a Democratic Congress is expected to accomplish little due to Presidential veto. Exit polls show 63% said the war in Iran was the wrong decision.
Tariffs: 66% of exit poll respondents said tariffs hurt the national economy, a read-through for Industrials and Consumer Discretionary.
AI regulation and data center policy: 76% of exit poll respondents oppose a new data center in their community, with Democrats more negative.

tension_points.bull_case: AAII sentiment, the US/non-US DM P/E at post-COVID lows, and forward P/E compression (24.5%) beyond the typical major-drawdown compression suggest the tier 1 pullback may be nearly done, with the low in before long if the midterm shock is just repricing.
tension_points.bear_case: Sentiment and valuation are not washed out. Russell 2000 P/Es are not at April 2025 lows, EPS revisions are decelerating and downward revisions could compress P/Es further, with AI policy risk to earnings still emerging.
tension_points.what_invalidates: A significant challenge to the earnings and economic outlook, likely visible in early 1Q27 year-ahead outlooks, would push the pullback into tier 2 (14-20%, S&P 6,255-6,724).

tension_points.bull_case: Small Caps have outperformed since mid-October on rotation out of big-cap Tech, with strong NFP support and consensus expecting Small Cap net income growth to lead the S&P 500 in early 2027.
tension_points.bear_case: Small Caps tend to underperform when volatility rises, spreads widen or jobs growth stalls, and may not lead in outright derisking. Russell 2000 valuations are not deeply oversold.
tension_points.what_invalidates: A widening in high yield spreads, a VIX rise beyond containment (the Iran war high was about 30) or a drawdown moving beyond tier 1.
